definition: Sentimental in an overdone, sickly sweet way that feels forced or insincere.
example: With its slow-motion hugs and swelling violins, the holiday commercial struck many viewers as mawkish.
nuance: Mawkish is harsher than sentimental: it says the feeling is so overdone that it turns sickly or embarrassing, never touching.
prompt: A critic reviews a novel whose final chapter is packed with tearful reunions.
options: The critic found the ending mawkish, with three tearful reunions in ten pages.
The critic praised the mawkish chapter for its restrained, understated emotion.
The critic called the chapter mawkish because its tangled plot twists were hard for readers to follow.
The critic called the chapter mawkish because it cruelly mocked its own characters.
reasons: Stacking up weepy scenes until the emotion feels forced is exactly what earns this label.
Restraint is the reverse; the word describes feeling that is laid on far too thick.
A confusing plot has nothing to do with gushing, excessive sentiment.
The word sounds a bit like "mocking," but it refers to syrupy emotion, not ridicule.

practice.prompt: A songwriter revises the lyrics of a ballad about her childhood home.
options: The mawkish lyrics were so spare and dry that listeners felt no emotion at all.
She chose a mawkish chord progression, which meant the guitar part was technically very difficult to play.
The ballad was mawkish in the best sense, moving listeners through honest, earned emotion.
Her first draft felt mawkish, so she cut the lines about tears falling like rain on the old porch.
reasons: Lyrics with no feeling are the opposite of emotion poured on too heavily.
How hard a part is to play says nothing about excessive sentiment.
The word is always critical; honest, earned feeling would be called poignant instead.
Spotting overwrought, syrupy imagery and trimming it uses the word correctly.
